newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Palladium gleams among dull commodities.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Palladium gleams among dull commodities.

text.p: Worries about delays to supply from Russia on Wednesday triggered a fresh rally in prices of palladium to their highest in 17 years.

Commodity markets were otherwise duller than of late, with gold, oil and industrial metals just easier and coffee futures volatile now that profit-taking has blown the froth of their recent spectacular advance.
Palladium prices exploded in a market squeezed by protracted delays in Russian supplies.
The rare white metal, used in electronics, catalytic converters and dentistry, fixed at $210 an ounce.By contrast its previous fix on Tuesday was $188.50.

"The market is extremely nervous about Russian deliveries. Palladium and platinum are much higher this morning even though there has really not being any fresh news," said analyst Hanspeter Hausheer of Swiss Bank Corp.
Gold fixed little changed at $341.75 an ounce in the London afternoon.
The gold market ignored the excitement in the platinum group metals (PGMs), as it did the German drama over plans to revalue gold reserves to qualify for European Monetary Union.
Industrial metals remained under pressure as investors reduce exposure to the sector ahead of the traditionally slow summer quarter in the Northern Hemisphere.
Late in London's day the three months delivery copper price had fallen to around $2,475 per tonne.

Coffee was volatile after last week's dramatic run-up to 20-year highs in New York. New York July arabica coffee futures, hit by speculative profit-taking in recent sessions, were around $2.55 per pound after the high at $3.18 last week.
Coffee trading on Wednesday began on the New York Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange with another speculative sell-off on news that Colombia opened "unlimited" July-August coffee export registrations.
But nervous buying on prospects of cool weather in Brazil, now in the season when it might have a damaging frost, and bargain hunting emerged.
Brazilian weather services on Wednesday were forecasting a cold weekend for key coffee regions, with temperatures possibly dropping to critical levels.
But Smith Barney meterologist Jon Davis said in his daily update there was little threat of frost or freeze damage in the next 10 days.
Benchmark London robusta coffee futures were also lower at $2,085 per tonne.
Oil markets were again slightly weaker on bearish data from the United States and the prospect of a speedy renewal of Iraq's "oil-for-food" deal.
Brent Blend crude, the world benchmark grade, was at one point down almost 15 cents $18.76 per barrel, just under the $19 average of the past three months.
Oil stocks rose nearly 17 million barrels in the United States last week to stand some 24 million barrels above year-ago levels, according to figures by the American Petroleum Institute (API).
The United Nations Security Council is also set to vote to extend an agreement to ease Gulf War sanctions on Iraq to let it sell more oil to buy food.
Grain prices were easier again on the Chicago Board of Trade, led by soybeans which fell amid speculation that the United States was importing more beans from Latin America.
Some key prices at 1700 GMT.
